title: Dee Gives Birth

jokes.text: Mac reveals he's been throwing their mail in the sewer because they never open it, and he didn't expect anyone to look for it there.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Mac emerge from a sewer holding filthy mail, everyone demands to know what their mail was doing in the sewer.
jokes.punchline: Mac admits he threw it there to hide it, explaining he never expected them to go rooting around in the sewer — which is itself a ridiculous expectation to have about anyone.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny escalating absurdism: the solution to a mundane problem (unopened mail) is insane, then the defense of that insane solution is even more insane. The logic — 'I'd never expect you to be in the sewer' — is perfectly deranged Mac-reasoning. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Look what Charlie and I found. Look at this.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, God. Ahh! Get that away from me. It reeks.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dude, this is our mail.

jokes.text: Charlie and Mac explain they hang out naked in the sewer, feeling around for rings and coins with their feet because 'it's almost like clamming.'
jokes.setup: Everyone demands to know what Charlie and Mac were doing in the sewer in the first place.
jokes.punchline: They hang out there regularly, strip naked so they don't get dirty, and forage for valuables with their feet — casually comparing it to clamming as if this is a perfectly reasonable leisure activity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a premier example of Always Sunny's specific absurdist genius. The escalation is perfect: sewer → naked in sewer → naked to stay clean → feeling for valuables with feet → 'it's almost like clamming.' The clamming analogy is what elevates it from weird to transcendent. It's completely Charlie-and-Mac specific — no other characters or show would generate this logic. The deadpan confidence with which they defend it makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I threw it in there. You turkeys never open it, so I just started throwing it in the sewer.

jokes.text: 'Rings, coins, nudity. That's all part of the fun.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are defending the sewer as a place of discovery, listing what they find.
jokes.punchline: 'Nudity' is listed as a found item alongside rings and coins, delivered matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: The list is well-constructed — 'rings, coins' sets up a treasure-hunt vibe, then 'nudity' as a found object completely reframes what's happening down there. Economy is excellent, delivered with total sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Because if I threw it in the trash, you would find it and then yell at me. Besides, I certainly never expected you guys to be rooting around in the sewer.

jokes.text: 'You feel it with your feet. It's almost like clamming. You mash around with your feet?'
jokes.setup: The gang presses for details on how exactly they find things naked in the sewer.
jokes.punchline: They compare it earnestly to clamming — a wholesome, family-friendly seaside activity — implying they mash around barefoot in sewage for treasure.
jokes.explanation: The comparison to 'clamming' is a genuinely funny juxtaposition — it normalizes something grotesque by using a mundane analogy. Dee's incredulous 'you mash around with your feet?' reaction beat makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We always go in the sewer. We hang out in the sewer.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: There's stuff down there.

jokes.text: Dee's water breaking interrupts the sewer conversation mid-sentence, cutting off Frank's question about the drain.
jokes.setup: Frank is mid-sentence asking about the sewer drain system when Dee announces her water broke.
jokes.punchline: Frank's absorbed sewer conversation is instantly, violently interrupted by actual medical urgency, underscoring how absurdly the gang prioritizes their weird interests.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed structural joke. The comic rule of three-ish escalation of the sewer conversation gets punctured by the most dramatic possible real-world event. It works because we've been lulled into the sewer discussion genuinely.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't knock the sewer till you've tried the sewer. You find shit down there.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: But how are you so clean?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We take our clothes off so we don't get dirty.

jokes.text: Dennis brags about hitting 120 mph driving to the hospital, while Mac says 'I almost stewed my drawers,' and Dennis complains Dee's screaming probably screwed up his transmission.
jokes.setup: They've rushed Dee to the hospital in an apparent emergency.
jokes.punchline: Dennis is proud of his reckless driving as an achievement; Mac is thrilled by it; Dennis's primary concern is damage to his car, not Dee's welfare.
jokes.explanation: Solid character-specific comedy. Dennis's narcissism expressed through concern for his transmission over his laboring sister is exactly his character. 'I almost stewed my drawers' is a funny Mac-ism. The juxtaposition of emergency and petty self-interest is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Big stuff. Rings, coins, nudity. That's part of the fun.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The two of you are walking around in the sewers naked looking for rings and coins?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You feel it with your feet. It's almost like clamming.

jokes.text: The gang immediately tries to dismiss themselves from the hospital — 'If we're off the hook, let's head back to the bar. Yeah, I could get blitzed.' — the moment Dee tells them there's no guy.
jokes.setup: Dee tells them there's no father in the picture and says she's got it handled.
jokes.punchline: Their instant, unanimous reaction is to leave and get drunk, with zero concern for their laboring friend/sister.
jokes.explanation: Dependable Always Sunny character comedy — the gang's callousness is their consistent defining trait. 'I could get blitzed' is a funny line. Not a surprising beat for this show, but executed crisply.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: My water just broke! I'm having a baby.

jokes.text: Dennis's argument for finding the dad: the baby 'ruined my transmission' and 'ruined a perfectly good sewer conversation,' and 'God knows what he's going to ruin in the future.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is convincing the group they need to find the father so the baby doesn't become their responsibility.
jokes.punchline: His list of the baby's crimes starts with the transmission and the sewer conversation — petty, ridiculous grievances treated as genuine injustices that necessitate finding the father.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the transmission and the sewer conversation landing as legitimate grievances against an unborn baby is sharp character writing. Dennis treating his car and his friends' absurd hobby as equivalent to genuine parental concern is perfectly him. 'God knows what he's going to ruin in the future' as a chilling prophecy about a baby is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: There's a baby inside of me running out of water. Look out!

jokes.text: Charlie's theory on conception: 'Any multiple number of sperms could have gone up there and eaten the egg.' Dennis corrects him: 'Sperm doesn't eat the egg.' Charlie: 'It doesn't eat the egg and grow strong and become a baby?'
jokes.setup: The gang speculates that there could be multiple fathers.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's understanding of reproduction involves sperm eating eggs and growing strong — like a Pac-Man/survival-of-the-fittest hybrid biology that is entirely wrong and also completely Charlie.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Charlie's confident, internally logical but completely wrong biology is a hallmark of his character — he's not stupid so much as operating on a parallel set of facts. 'It doesn't eat the egg and grow strong and become a baby?' has perfect rhythm and cadence. The delivery of this as genuine, earnest curiosity rather than a joke makes it funnier. It's deeply Charlie-specific; this joke cannot exist without his character.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You hit 120! 120!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I almost stewed my drawers. She was screaming in my ear. Probably screwed my transmission up.

jokes.text: The gang decides who stays at the hospital by the fact that one person is on the wrong side of the room: 'Mostly because, you know, we're all on this side and you're over there... You didn't make it to the side on time.'
jokes.setup: Someone needs to stay with Dee at the hospital.
jokes.punchline: The 'decision' is made entirely by arbitrary physical positioning — whoever failed to drift to one side of the room is stuck with the job, and this is treated as a fully legitimate democratic process.
jokes.explanation: Classic gang decision-making comedy — their completely arbitrary, self-serving logic presented as fair and reasonable. The escalating justification ('also, now we're backing out') is well-constructed. Standard Always Sunny fare, executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's no guy?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: There's no guy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's complicated.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's gotta be a guy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We'll go get the guy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We'll get the dad.

jokes.text: Dennis corrects Mac flatly: 'No, sperm doesn't eat the egg.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just described sperm eating the egg and growing strong into a baby.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's correction is completely dry and immediate, implying this is not the first time he's had to correct Mac's biology.
jokes.explanation: Works as a tag to joke #13. The flatness of the correction is the joke — Dennis doesn't even sound exasperated, just weary. Scores high on economy because it does its job in six words.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Why don't you guys do what you do best and don't care, okay? I got it from here. We can take it from here. Right, Michael?

jokes.text: Dee, heavily pregnant, is standing on top of a rolling chair trying to reach the TV.
jokes.setup: Dennis enters Dee's hospital room.
jokes.punchline: Dee, in active labor, is on a rolling chair reaching for the TV — a visual of spectacular self-destructive stupidity.
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag. Dee's chaotic self-sabotage is pure character comedy — she's in labor and her priority is her soap operas, and she's endangering herself and the baby to get them. The image of a heavily pregnant woman on a rolling chair is inherently slapstick.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The brunt of the responsibility of this kid is gonna fall on us. We're gonna have to do everything. Look what she was doing with the mail, for Christ sakes.

jokes.text: Dennis's lecture to Dee: 'You are an irresponsible person who stands atop rolling chairs and chooses to go flying through windows. Have the baby first. Have the stupid baby, then go flying through all the windows you like.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is admonishing Dee for being on the rolling chair.
jokes.punchline: His parenting-style lecture grants her full permission to go flying through windows post-partum — as if that's the reasonable compromise, treating window-flying as her established hobby.
jokes.explanation: Very strong joke. Dennis's condescending, faux-responsible tone combined with the absurdist concession 'then go flying through all the windows you like' is perfectly constructed. The idea that flying through windows is simply a behavior she enjoys that just needs to be timed correctly is a great comedic logic. High quotability — this line has the shape and rhythm of something people repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Look what this kid has ruined already. He's ruined my transmission.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He's ruined a perfectly good sewer conversation.

jokes.text: Dennis, wrestling with the TV: 'I'll figure you out, you son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has promised to fix Dee's TV situation and is now struggling with the hospital television.
jokes.punchline: His intense, antagonistic address of the inanimate TV as a worthy adversary — 'you son of a bitch' — reveals his pathological need to dominate everything, including electronics.
jokes.explanation: Short but effective. Dennis's narcissism making him adversarial even with a TV is a small but efficient character beat. Economy is excellent — the line does a lot in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Any multiple number of sperms could have gone up there and eaten the egg. There could be so many dads.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, sperm doesn't eat the egg.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It doesn't eat the egg and grow strong and become a baby?

jokes.text: Frank forgot to bring beer to the 'party' he organized to interrogate Dee's potential baby daddies, then defends it: 'We don't want them thinking it's an interrogation.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie arrive at Frank's 'party' to find no beer, and Frank explains he forgot it.
jokes.punchline: Frank's concern is maintaining the illusion of a party (not an interrogation), but he forgot the one item that would most convincingly make it look like a party.
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the party-as-interrogation running gag. The irony of a coverup party with no beer is a good foundational joke. Not a standout but it establishes the premise efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, mostly because we're all on this side. You're over there. Just 'cause you guys made it to one side before me? You didn't make it to this side on time.

jokes.text: Cricket arrives at the party — 'Who invited Cricket?' 'I did, because I figured it's a wild card.' Mac: 'That's a stone you can leave unturned.'
jokes.setup: Cricket appears at the party among the potential baby daddies.
jokes.punchline: Frank invited Cricket as a 'wild card,' which Mac dismisses as an entirely unnecessary gamble — Cricket's presence as a potential Dee sexual partner is the dark joke.
jokes.explanation: Cricket's recurring role as a destitute wild card whose sexual involvement with Dee is treated as a horrifying but plausible possibility is good dark character comedy. 'That's a stone you can leave unturned' is a funny malapropism-adjacent twist on the idiom.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You are standing on top of a rolling chair. You're gonna go flying through that window, for God sakes. Get down.

jokes.text: Bill the sex addict: 'That's why I had a vasectomy.' He winks. 'You just winked when you said that.' 'Did you have a vasectomy or not?' 'No. But that's what I would tell the ladies, so I didn't have to wear a condom.'
jokes.setup: In an interrogation disguised as guy talk about hating condoms, Bill claims he had a vasectomy as his reason for not wearing them.
jokes.punchline: The wink gives it away — he never had a vasectomy; he lies about having one to avoid condoms. As a self-identified sex addict, this is revealed as a predatory manipulation tactic.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed joke. The visual tell (the wink) precedes the verbal reveal, which is a smart structural choice. The revelation escalates naturally — sex addict → no condoms → vasectomy → wink → actually lied about vasectomy to avoid condoms. It's dark and funny simultaneously, which is Always Sunny's sweet spot.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I have a very specific birth plan and mostly it involves me watching my stories to relax but I can't get this goddamn TV to do anything.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That is incredibly shady.' Then immediately: 'What a beautiful underhanded thing.'
jokes.setup: Bill reveals he lied about having a vasectomy to avoid condoms.
jokes.punchline: Mac starts to moralize ('incredibly shady') then immediately pivots to genuine admiration ('beautiful underhanded thing'), revealing his actual values.
jokes.explanation: Tight, efficient character joke. The pivot from performative disgust to authentic admiration is the whole joke, delivered in two lines. Mac's moral posturing immediately collapsing is very on-brand. 'Beautiful underhanded thing' is a memorable phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Have the baby first. Have the stupid baby. Then go flying through all the windows you like.

jokes.text: Dennis delivers the 'hammer of Thor / thunder of my vengeance will echo through these corridors like the dust of a thousand winds' speech to a nurse.
jokes.setup: Dennis is demanding a working TV and a new room for Dee from a hospital nurse.
jokes.punchline: His threat escalates into an utterly unhinged piece of purple prose — 'the dust of a thousand winds' — delivered with complete sincerity, which a weary nurse dismisses with 'I don't have time for this.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. Dennis's grandiosity expressing itself through increasingly incoherent epic metaphors — 'the dust of a thousand winds' makes no logical sense as a simile for echoing thunder, which is exactly why it's funny. His complete, unselfconscious sincerity while saying something objectively ridiculous is Dennis at his best. High quotability; this is the kind of line Always Sunny fans repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: God, this baby is becoming such an irritating thing to me. Yeah. God, what an irritating thing babies are.

jokes.text: The nurse's response to Dennis's Thor speech: 'I ain't going to jail over you. I will beat your ass and think nothing of it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has delivered his grandiose Thor threat to the nurse.
jokes.punchline: Instead of being cowed, the nurse responds with a credible, completely unimpressed threat of physical violence — suggesting Dennis's intimidation tactics have zero effect on people with actual problems.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation of Dennis's pomposity. The nurse's flat, genuine threat ('I will beat your ass and think nothing of it') is funnier than any clever retort would be. The specificity of 'I ain't going to jail over you' — implying she's genuinely calculated the legal risk — is brilliant. Works as both a standalone joke and as a payoff to Dennis's speech.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: How are we supposed to know this is a party if there's no beer? A party with no beer.

jokes.text: Dee has left the hospital while in labor to get a sandwich because she was 'kind of hungry' and 'getting bored.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is looking for Dee and finds her wandering the hospital corridor.
jokes.punchline: She left her labor room mid-delivery to satisfy mundane needs — hunger and boredom — with no apparent awareness that this is dangerous or unusual.
jokes.explanation: Good Dee character comedy. Her complete absence of appropriate concern for her own medical situation, mixed with mundane priorities (sandwich, boredom), is funny and consistent with her chaotic selfishness. 'Mostly, I was just getting bored' is a great throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We don't want them thinking it's an interrogation.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Oh! Hey! Party! Party! All right! Hey!

jokes.text: The hospital has put a stranger — an apparently dead old man with 'paper skin' — in Dee's room because she wasn't using it.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee return to her room to find a strange man lying in her bed.
jokes.punchline: The hospital's pragmatic solution to Dee abandoning her room is to slide in another patient — apparently a dying (or dead) old man. The logic is bleak hospital bureaucracy taken to its darkest endpoint.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy done well. The hospital putting a potentially dead man in a laboring woman's room because the bed was 'going to waste' is grimly logical and funny. 'Paper skin' as a descriptor is a good specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Who invited Cricket? I did, because I figured it's a wild card. That's a stone you can leave unturned.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Is he dead? Dennis, is he dead?' — then tries to 'jiggle his ankle' to determine if he's alive, and upon touching him says 'He's very cold.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Dennis discover the apparently lifeless old man in her hospital room.
jokes.punchline: Dee's diagnostic method is ankle-jiggling; her report back is delivered in the same complaining tone she uses for everything — 'He's very cold' — as if 'very cold' is an inconvenience rather than evidence of death.
jokes.explanation: Solid dark comedy with good Dee characterization. Her ankle-jiggling methodology and the flat delivery of 'He's very cold' treat potential death as a minor inconvenience. Consistent with the show's tone.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: It's good to get away from the wife and kids for a little bit- let the hair down.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So you're still with your wife after all that shit with Dee?

jokes.text: Dee: 'Why would they put a dead old man with paper skin in my room when I'm trying to give birth?' — then Dennis explains it's because she wasn't using the room.
jokes.setup: It's confirmed the old man may be dead and sharing Dee's room.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's explanation — 'because you weren't using the room, Dee, and the hospital is very full' — is delivered with complete reasonableness, as if this is satisfactory and logical.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Dee's earlier abandonment of her room. Dennis's reasonable-sounding explanation for why a dead man is in her labor room is a funny piece of dark logic. Slightly repetitive of the previous dead-man jokes but adds a satisfying callback layer.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You don't mind if I write some of this down, do you?

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: For what?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Just keeping a log of the party. We like to do that. A funny conversation pops up, you wanna remember it.

jokes.text: Dennis's explanation for why they put the dead man there: 'Because you weren't using the room, Dee, and the hospital is very full.'
jokes.setup: Dee is outraged a dead man was placed in her room.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the hospital's probable logic completely straight, as if it's a reasonable administrative decision. 'You weren't using the room' treats corpse-storage like overflow parking.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan logic is the joke. Dennis presenting corpse room-sharing as a sensible capacity management solution — with zero irony — is perfectly dark. It also retroactively justifies Dee's leaving as the cause of her problem.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I cannot stand the feel of a condom on my dick. I hate condoms. Hate 'em, hate 'em, hate 'em, hate 'em. The three of us just don't use 'em. How about you?

jokes.text: Bill's ex with Dee: 'She contacted me for a while. Usually when she was drunk.' — 'Drunken late-night booty calls?' — 'No. She usually just yells at me, calls me names, like army jerk, camo turkey.'
jokes.setup: Mac assumes Dee's late-night drunk contacts were booty calls.
jokes.punchline: Instead of seduction, Dee's method is to drunkenly hurl creative but oddly specific insults ('army jerk,' 'camo turkey') at men until they give her sex.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke, one of the episode's best. The reveal that Dee's seduction technique is drunken insult-hurling ('army jerk,' 'camo turkey') is a perfect character-specific absurdity. The specificity of the insults is what makes it — not generic mean names, but oddly military-themed half-insults that are more confusing than cutting. The misdirection from 'booty calls' to 'name-calling as foreplay' is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: That's why I had a vasectomy, guys.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You had a vasectomy?

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Yep.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You just winked when you said that. Did you have a vasectomy or not?

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: No. But that's what I would tell the ladies so I didn't have to wear a condom.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie comfort a crying Bill, then immediately tell him to stop crying because 'you're a soldier, and you should be tougher.'
jokes.setup: Bill gets emotional after being confronted about his relationship with Dee.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's version of comfort is to validate him for a half-second then tell him to stop crying because soldiers don't cry, before he even leaves the room.
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. The gang's total inability to actually provide comfort, pivoting immediately to insults, is consistent. Not the sharpest joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: If you do not get my sister her stories and a new room as soon as possible then I will come down on this hospital like the hammer of Thor. The thunder of my vengeance will echo through these corridors like the gust of a thousand winds!

jokes.text: Charlie and Mac quietly side-eye the crying soldier: 'This is the guy who's defending our country?' 'Well, he's definitely a candidate.'
jokes.setup: Bill leaves after being told to get a grip.
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'he's definitely a candidate' — referring to the paternity question — is delivered as genuine measured consideration despite everything they've seen, which is funnier than outright dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Economical joke. 'He's definitely a candidate' works on both levels — paternity and military. Good deadpan from Mac. Brief but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't have time for this. I ain't going to jail over you. I will beat your ass and think nothing of it. I'm not doing this with you today. I'm not! I'm not!

jokes.text: Frank is high at his own interrogation-party and doesn't even know what he's high on: 'Are you high on blow?' 'Whatever Duncan gave me.' 'You don't even know what you're high on?' 'No.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie discover the state of Frank's interrogation party.
jokes.punchline: Frank is high on an unknown substance given to him by one of the suspects at his own investigation party — no curiosity about what it is.
jokes.explanation: Good Frank comedy. His complete passivity about not knowing what he's on — 'whatever Duncan gave me,' delivered flatly — is perfectly Frank. The investigator being unknowingly drugged by his suspect is a nice comic situation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You left the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah. I was kind of hungry. Mostly I was just getting bored.

jokes.text: Mac gestures to a Korean busboy: 'Is that the bus boy from the Korean restaurant?' Frank: 'Yeah, yeah. She banged him.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie survey the eclectic guest list at the party — potential Dee baby daddies.
jokes.punchline: The list of Dee's sexual partners is revealed to include a random Korean restaurant busboy, delivered with complete casualness by Frank.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag beat. The expanding and increasingly unlikely list of Dee's partners is funny, and Frank's breezy confirmation 'yeah, she banged him' is a good deadpan delivery. The randomness of the busboy is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Why is there a strange man in my room?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They probably slid this man in here thinking that you were never gonna use the room.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I don't want there to be a strange man laying in my room who looks dead.

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee do a Weekend at Bernie's with the dead old man — putting sunglasses on him, waving his arm — while Dennis justifies it: 'Without the sunglasses, Weekend at Bernie's would have been very dark.' 'Yeah. Strange movie. Very strange tale.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee need to move a potentially dead man out of her room and have dressed him up in sunglasses to make it look like he's alive.
jokes.punchline: In the middle of their Weekend at Bernie's operation, Dennis delivers a deadpan film critique of Weekend at Bernie's itself, treating it as a genuinely interesting cinematic analysis rather than acknowledging the absurdity of their current situation.
jokes.explanation: Very strong joke. Dennis's sincere film criticism of Weekend at Bernie's while actively performing a Weekend at Bernie's on a potentially dead hospital patient is a great piece of meta-absurdism. 'Without the sunglasses it would have been very dark' — 'very strange tale' — these work as actual observations AND as oblivious commentary on their own situation. The deadpan commitment to the movie discussion is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm gonna scream in his face and see if he wakes up.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Do not scream in the man's face.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'll jiggle his ankle, and that will determine whether he's alive or not.

jokes.text: Options for disposing of the old man: 'Are we just gonna throw him in the trash, or are we gonna find, like, a laundry shoot, fire him down that?' — 'Maybe we could stuff him in a drawer, or, like, jam him in a closet.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are trying to dispose of/relocate the old man's body.
jokes.punchline: Their disposal options are brainstormed with the same pragmatic casualness as moving furniture — trash, laundry chute, drawer, closet — with no ethical consideration for the man.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating dark comedy. Each disposal option is worse than the last (trash → laundry chute → drawer → closet), and they're all delivered as reasonable brainstorming. 'Fire him down that' is a funny verb choice for a human body.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Why would they put a dead old man with paper skin in my room when I'm trying to give birth?

jokes.text: The old man is revealed to be alive: 'Please don't put me in the trash!'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee have been treating the old man as definitely dead, brainstorming ways to dispose of his body.
jokes.punchline: He's been alive and listening to their disposal plans the whole time, and his only objection is the specific option of the trash.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the most economically perfect reveals in the episode. Everything hinges on 'Please don't put me in the trash!' — five words that pay off the entire dead-man arc, reveal he's been conscious throughout, and imply he's maybe fine with the other options. The joke is built from an impeccably constructed setup and delivers maximum surprise. The specificity of 'the trash' as his only objection is the final touch.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: This was not part of my birth plan. This was not part of my birth plan, sir.

jokes.text: Dee flat-out refuses to share a room with 'an old man who likes to pretend to be dead. He's a liar.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Craig is revealed to be alive. The nurse arrives.
jokes.punchline: Dee's response is not relief that he's alive — it's outrage that he 'pretended' to be dead, calling him a liar. She characterizes his near-death/unconsciousness as a deliberate deception aimed at her.
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-centered response to discovering a nearly-dead old man is alive is perfect character comedy. 'He's a liar' reframes his condition as a personal affront. Only Dee would be angry at someone for not being dead.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What's the deal here, bud?

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.line: Well, no, she contacted me for a while usually when she was drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Drunken late-night booty calls?

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.line: No. She usually just yells at me calls me names like army jerk, camo turkey.

jokes.text: Dee: 'I flat-out refuse to share a room with an old man who likes to pretend to be dead. He's a liar.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Craig is revealed to be alive, not dead.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately reframes the situation as the old man being a dishonest prankster ('pretend to be dead') and declares him a 'liar,' ignoring that she and Dennis just tried to stuff him in a drawer.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dee moment. Her complete moral inversion — the man who was nearly thrown in a trash can by her is recast as the wrongdoer for 'pretending' to be dead — is perfect character comedy. 'He's a liar' is said with genuine indignation. It's a great capsule of Dee's pathological inability to acknowledge her own culpability. 'He's a liar' is very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.line: Sometimes she tricks me.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She tricks you?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She tricks you how?

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.line: To give her sex. She's a very manipulative person.

jokes.text: The nurse returns: 'You get your narrow ass back in that waiting room before I knock you in there. You have done enough today. Crazy ass white boy steadily dressing up folk and talking about Thor.'
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to follow Dee into the delivery room.
jokes.punchline: The nurse calls back Dennis's earlier Thor speech and his Weekend at Bernie's operation on Mr. Craig ('dressing up folk') as evidence that he has 'done enough today,' threatening him with physical removal.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The nurse's callback summary of Dennis's greatest hits — 'dressing up folk and talking about Thor' — is a perfect comedic recap that recontextualizes his absurd behavior from the outside. 'Crazy ass white boy' grounds it in a real-world perspective that makes it funnier. It's also a great double callback. 'Steady dressing up folk' is a memorable phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.line: Are you guys mad at me?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, man, we're not mad. Pull it together, because you're a soldier and you should be tougher.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie, in the waiting room, have a genuine emotional moment about the baby — then Mr. Craig interrupts with 'Please don't throw me in the trash.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are having an unexpectedly sincere moment about the impending baby.
jokes.punchline: Mr. Craig's anxious reminder — 'Please don't throw me in the trash' — punctures the sentimentality with his paranoid request, implying he's still traumatized from the earlier conversation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of a running gag. The emotional moment is set up — something rare for these characters — then punctured by Mr. Craig's paranoid repetition of his one concern. The fact that he keeps bringing it up suggests the trauma was real. The juxtaposition of genuine sentimentality and 'please don't throw me in the trash' is a great rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This is the guy that's defending our country?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, he's definitely a candidate.

jokes.text: Frank and Dennis have a sincere moment about the baby — interrupted by Mr. Craig: 'Please don't throw me in the trash.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Frank are having an unexpectedly touching moment about the impending birth.
jokes.punchline: Mr. Craig's voice from the background: 'Please don't throw me in the trash.' — He's still worried about this.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'trash' gag works as a running joke because the timing is perfect — it interrupts a sincere emotional beat, and Mr. Craig's continued anxiety about trash disposal implies he's still not entirely sure these people won't do it. Good escalation of the original joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What are your bridge friends doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You gotta give it the illusion of a party. It's gotta be a guy's night, that's why.

jokes.text: Mac's soliloquy about his old jean shorts: 'I slept in them shits, man. Eventually, I blew the crotch out of them things, but you can't wear 'em every day and expect for 'em to hold up. That was some nice ass denim, too. I miss those shorts. But you got to take 'em off every now and then.'
jokes.setup: Mac is in the hospital waiting room, apparently noticing Mr. Craig's jean shorts, which triggers a nostalgic monologue.
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers a sincere, detailed eulogy for his old jean shorts — including that he 'blew the crotch out of them' — ending with the profound wisdom 'you got to take 'em off every now and then,' implying he hadn't been.
jokes.explanation: Excellent weird character moment. Mac eulogizing his old jean shorts with genuine passion, grief, and hard-won wisdom — 'you got to take 'em off every now and then' — in a hospital waiting room while his friend is in labor is perfectly absurdist. 'I blew the crotch out of them things' is a great specific detail. The monologue's total non sequitur nature, delivered with sincerity, is very Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you high on blow?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Whatever Duncan gave me.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You don't even know what you're high on?

jokes.text: Frank's monologue about Jean shorts: 'I used to have some Jean shorts like that... I slept in them shits, man. Eventually, I blew the crotch out of them things.'
jokes.setup: Frank is in the waiting room, apparently musing while looking at someone (possibly Mr. Craig or his own reflection).
jokes.punchline: Frank delivers an unsolicited, oddly specific memoir about a beloved pair of Jean shorts, including that he 'blew the crotch out' by wearing them too often.
jokes.explanation: Pure Frank. A completely unprompted, deeply personal Jean shorts eulogy is exactly the kind of non-sequitur Frank delivers best. 'I slept in them shits, man' and 'blew the crotch out' are vivid, funny specific details. High character integration — only Frank has this internal world.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What is L'il Kev doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You gotta throw out a big net to catch the fish that she was banging.

jokes.text: Rex explains he has sex with Dee because she gets drunk and calls him names like 'cardio-jerk' or 'workout turkey,' and 'after a while I just kind of cave in.' Mac: 'Wow, you just... All right, I got to try that with someone.'
jokes.setup: Rex is being interrogated about his relationship with Dee.
jokes.punchline: The confirmation that Dee's drunk-insult seduction technique works (Rex confirms it, using 'cardio-jerk' and 'workout turkey' as the specific insults) and Mac's immediate takeaway is to adopt it himself.
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff to the 'drunk insult' bit. The expansion of Dee's insult vocabulary with new workout-themed entries ('cardio-jerk,' 'workout turkey') and the confirmation that this actually works is funny. Mac's takeaway — wanting to try it himself — is perfect character comedy. It also reveals something absurdly true about Dee: she can only seem to insult people within specific professional categories of the person.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Are you sure we're not taking this Weekend at Bernie's thing too far? I'm worried the sunglasses are ridiculous. The sunglasses lighten the mood. Make the whole thing feel like a fun, fun romp.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie summarize Dee's love life: 'She's slammin' ass all over town.' 'She's stuck on her curse words — "jerk" and "turkey" are all that she's using.' 'Yeah, well, clearly they're working for her, 'cause Rex is a quality lay.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie debrief after interviewing Rex.
jokes.punchline: Their analysis pivots between moralizing about Dee's vocabulary limitations and genuinely assessing Rex's quality as a sexual partner — 'Rex is a quality lay' — said with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. 'Rex is a quality lay' delivered with complete sincerity as a genuine data point in their analysis is funny. Mac and Charlie treating Dee's sex life as an investigative problem to solve — including commentary on the quality of participants — is good genre-aware comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Without the sunglasses Weekend at Bernie's would have been very dark. Yeah. Strange movie. Strange tale.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie spiral into parenting advice that includes 'don't have 'em doing cocaine,' 'get them off the Internet,' 'give 'em some books' — immediately countered with 'you don't want 'em to be a nerd.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie conclude none of the potential fathers are fit to parent, then try to articulate what good parenting looks like.
jokes.punchline: Their parenting philosophy immediately collapses into contradiction — cocaine bad, books bad (nerds), Internet bad — as they're simultaneously making the case they'd be better fathers.
jokes.explanation: Good sustained absurdist character comedy. The parenting advice list being mostly terrible or self-defeating is funny. The cocaine line sets the bar appropriately low for their parenting standards.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What's our plan here? Are we just gonna throw him in the trash or find a laundry chute Fire him down that?

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Craig
dialogue.line: Please don't put me in the trash.

jokes.text: The gang's parenting philosophy includes: 'don't have 'em doing cocaine,' 'off the Internet,' 'bash nerds'
jokes.setup: Emboldened by cocaine, Mac and Charlie debate what it takes to be a good parent.
jokes.punchline: Their parenting rules are a chaotic mix of genuine advice ('get them off the Internet') and violence ('bash nerds,' 'I'm gonna bash his head in if it's a nerd').
jokes.explanation: The gang's coke-fueled parenting philosophy is a great escalating sequence. 'If it's a nerd, I'm gonna bash his head in. Nerds get nowhere in life' is delivered with the genuine conviction of someone who believes it. The transition from mild guidelines to immediate nerd-bashing enthusiasm is a good escalation arc.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh, are you alive? Oh, my goodness. What is going on here? What are you doing with Mr. Craig?

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Craig
dialogue.line: They're trying to put me in the trash.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie threaten to 'bash nerds': 'If it's a nerd, I'm gonna bash his head in. Nerds get nowhere in life.' — 'I could bash some nerds right now.' — 'Well, right after this we should probably bash nerds.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are discussing what they'd do if the child is a nerd.
jokes.punchline: Their anti-nerd rhetoric escalates from hypothetical to immediate desire — 'I could bash some nerds right now' — with 'right after this' as a logical to-do item.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny escalation. The nerd-bashing impulse building to 'right after this we should probably bash nerds' as a scheduled activity is good character comedy. It's not the sharpest joke in the episode but the escalation is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh! It doesn't feel good. This sucks. This sucks a bag of dicks.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'That's all that parenting is. Pretending you know what you're talking about and then jamming it down a kid's throat.' — 'Oh, my God, that's what we're gonna do.'
jokes.setup: Mac says he and Charlie have great opinions about parenting.
jokes.punchline: Charlie accidentally articulates a cynically accurate theory of parenting — 'pretending you know and jamming it down a kid's throat' — which Mac receives as a profound revelation and actionable plan.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's smarter jokes. Charlie's theory is accidentally insightful and also accurately describes terrible parenting. The fact that it's immediately received as a revelation and battle plan is perfect. 'Jamming it down a kid's throat' as a parenting methodology is a great image.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Get your narrow ass back in that waiting room before I knock you in there. You have done enough today. Crazy-ass white boy steadily dressing up folk and talking about Thor.

jokes.text: Frank explains to Dennis why all the men are there: 'I couldn't decide who the dad was, so I brought everybody.' Dennis: 'You didn't even try and decide who the dad was, you just got high!' Frank: 'Well, the interrogation did turn into a coke party.'
jokes.setup: Dennis arrives to find the hospital room full of random men.
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation — 'the interrogation did turn into a coke party' — is delivered with complete Frank-ian lack of embarrassment, as if this is a natural and foreseeable evolution of events.
jokes.explanation: Great Frank line. 'The interrogation did turn into a coke party' has perfect economy and the word 'did' implies both acknowledgment and inevitability — of course it did. It's completely Frank. Very quotable, capturing his philosophy of life in nine words.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I used to have some jean shorts like that too. I slept in them shits, man. Eventually, I blew the crotch out of them things. But you can't wear 'em every day and expect for 'em to hold up. That was some nice-ass denim too. I miss them shorts. But you gotta take 'em off every now and then. You gotta take 'em off, son.

jokes.text: Mac's 'My Two Dads' vs. 'Three Men and a Baby' debate over co-dad arrangements
jokes.setup: Dennis wants to join Mac and Charlie as a co-father. They debate the structure.
jokes.punchline: The debate centers on whether this is a 'My Two Dads' situation or a 'Three Men and a Baby' situation — referencing two specific TV/film properties to determine how many dads are optimal.
jokes.explanation: Using 80s pop culture as a framework for multi-dad logistics is a good bit. 'An equally effective movie, right? A great movie' — the digression into film criticism mid-paternity crisis is very true to these characters.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why are you having sex with her?

dialogue.speaker: Rex
dialogue.line: Well, she gets drunk and calls me a cardio-jerk or a workout turkey. And after a while, I just kind of cave in.

jokes.text: Bill, upon hearing he might be the father: 'If this kid is mine, I'm gonna blow my brains out.' Then collapses, apparently too high: 'He took an eight-ball to the dome.'
jokes.setup: Bill is told there will be blood tests to determine paternity.
jokes.punchline: Bill's extreme reaction to potential fatherhood — threatening suicide — is immediately one-upped by him apparently overdoing cocaine at the party and collapsing, with Frank delivering the clinical diagnosis 'he took an eight-ball to the dome.'
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy escalation. The threat of suicide being immediately superseded by an actual medical crisis via cocaine is a good dark-comedy one-two. 'He took an eight-ball to the dome' is a great Frank-ism, clinical and street-informed simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She's just berating these guys into having sex with her.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, and she is slammin' ass all over town.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She's getting way more action than us.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: She's stuck on her curse words. 'Jerk' and 'turkey' are all that she's using.

jokes.text: 'We're gonna be the father of the baby now.' 'Yes, we're gonna be the fathers.' 'It has been decided. So sayeth Thor.' 'Thor said it.' — followed immediately by the others asking who Thor is.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie announce their decision to be the father(s) of the baby.
jokes.punchline: Dennis invokes Thor again as divine authority for the decision, but his callback lands flat even with the other characters — no one recognizes the reference, and Dennis is forced to admit his earlier Thor line 'sounded a lot cooler than that.'
jokes.explanation: Good meta-callback. Dennis trying to reprise his Thor bit and it not landing even in-universe is a funny piece of self-aware comedy. 'So sayeth Thor' has less energy than the original, and even Dennis seems to feel it. The in-universe failure of the callback mirrors the comedic diminishing returns of callbacks generally.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Kids spend all their time on the Internet. 'Hi. Who are you? There's your penis and there's your butt.' You gotta learn from some books. You don't want 'em reading too many books. You don't want 'em to be a nerd.

jokes.text: Dennis recaps his earlier achievements with pride: 'I busted out this sweet Thor line on this lady... I mean, I really hit her with it. And I never reference the nordic gods.' — The others: 'What are you saying, though? I don't understand what your point is.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining why he's now excited about fatherhood.
jokes.punchline: His evidence for being 'fired on all cylinders' is the Thor speech and the Weekend at Bernie's operation — moments the audience knows were embarrassing — delivered with complete self-satisfaction. The others have no idea what he's talking about.
jokes.explanation: Good Dennis narcissism beat. His completely delusional self-assessment — the Thor line was bad, the Weekend at Bernie's was bizarre — is funny, and the others' polite bafflement is a good reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: If it's a nerd, I'm gonna bash his head in. Nerds get nowhere in life. Oh, my God. Is he a nerd? I could bash some nerds right now. Right after this we should probably bash nerds. I gotta get it out of my system.

jokes.text: The 'Three Men and a Baby' discussion: someone suggests folding Dennis in to make it three dads, comparing it favorably to 'My Two Dads' — 'An equally effective movie, right? A great movie.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie had planned a 'My Two Dads' situation but Dennis also wants to be the father.
jokes.punchline: They pivot to 'Three Men and a Baby' as the superior model, treating it as a legitimate parenting framework, then give 'Three Men and a Baby' a sincere film endorsement ('equally effective,' 'great movie') as if movie precedent is a valid basis for parental arrangement.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist comedy. The gang planning their parenting arrangement based on TV show and movie templates, then seriously rating the films as parenting models, is a good joke. 'An equally effective movie' implies they've actually weighed the two film's effectiveness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We have a lot of ideas about raising a kid. We are men who can be great dads. We have great opinions.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And that's all that parenting is - pretending you know what you're talking about and then jamming it down a kid's throat.

jokes.text: The reveal that Carmen (a transgender woman) is there to collect her baby — Dee was the surrogate. Frank: 'Oh, yeah. The tranny's the dad.'
jokes.setup: The whole episode has been built around finding the mysterious father of Dee's baby, with the gang interrogating her entire sexual history.
jokes.punchline: The father is Carmen, a recurring transgender character — Dee was a surrogate the whole time, and there never was a traditional 'guy.' Frank's summary 'the tranny's the dad' cuts through all the confusion with brutal simplicity.
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural crown jewel. The entire episode's premise — finding the father — is dismantled by a reveal that recontextualizes everything. Dee wasn't being coy about the father; she was a surrogate. The gang's elaborate investigation (the coke party, the interrogations, the insult-seduction analysis) was completely unnecessary. The episode's climax earns its impact through sustained misdirection across the full runtime. The reveal itself is well-calibrated: surprising but retrospectively logical.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Charlie and I have decided that we are going to be the father of this child.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, we did a complete 180.

jokes.text: Mac, Charlie, and Dennis's reaction to the surrogate reveal: 'Dee, you tricked us?' — 'Well, we were getting all pumped up about being this baby's dad.' — 'This has been a huge disappointment for us.'
jokes.setup: Dee explains she was a surrogate and never tricked anyone.
jokes.punchline: The gang's grievance is not concern for Dee or the baby, but that their excitement at being fathers was wasted — 'a huge disappointment for us' — framing the entire birth as an inconvenience to their emotional arc.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. The gang treating their own thwarted daddy fantasy as the actual tragedy of the situation is funny and consistent. 'This has been a huge disappointment for us' is a good line, though the joke is a touch predictable at this point in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I did this Weekend at Bernie's operation earlier that would have blown you guys' minds - it was very effective. Then I busted out this sweet Thor line on this lady because she was pissing me off. It was, like, boom! I really hit her with it. And I never reference the Nordic gods.

jokes.text: Mac: 'We were gonna be great dads. We were gonna impose our will on the kid. We had a three men and a baby thing going on!'
jokes.setup: Mac is processing the disappointment of not being fathers.
jokes.punchline: His list of lost fatherhood opportunities leads with 'impose our will on the kid' — revealing what his vision of parenting actually was — before the film framework callback.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that consolidates the parenting subplot. 'We were gonna impose our will on the kid' as the primary loss is a great character-specific grievance — it accidentally reveals their actual parenting goals.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Then I busted out this sweet Thor line on this lady because she was pissing me off. It was, like, boom! I really hit her with it. And I never reference the Nordic gods.

jokes.text: Dennis's moment of unexpected growth: 'I have to admit, this whole thing might be for the best. I mean, those two are gonna make great parents, much better parents than any of us would, don't you think?' — The group grudgingly agrees.
jokes.setup: Everyone is processing that they won't be fathers.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's surprisingly mature moment — acknowledging Carmen and her partner will be better parents — is immediately followed by everyone agreeing a baby 'would've screwed up our chemistry,' rationalizing away any genuine growth.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny 'almost learned something' beat. The characters approach genuine growth then immediately retreat. 'It would've screwed up our chemistry' as the real reason they're relieved is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Maybe instead of doing a My Two Dads type thing we could fold in another dad and do a Three Men and a Baby type situation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I like that.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: An equally effective movie.

jokes.text: Dennis to Dee: 'That being said, don't get knocked up anymore, Dee. It's getting old.'
jokes.setup: The resolution of the episode's events.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's parting wisdom to his sister who just gave birth as a surrogate is to stop getting pregnant — delivered as if this is a reasonable and fair criticism of a pattern of behavior.
jokes.explanation: Solid Dennis line. 'It's getting old' implies this is a recurring behavior pattern, which is funnier than it being the first time. His complete failure to register the surrogate distinction ('knocked up' rather than 'gave birth as a surrogate') is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I couldn't decide who the dad was, so I brought everybody.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You didn't try and decide who the dad was. You just got high.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, the interrogation did turn into a coke party.

jokes.text: Frank tries to work out the genetics: 'The mother is the father and the father is black and the baby's not black, so...' Dennis: 'It's all been explained.' Frank: 'I'll talk you through it later.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is wrapping up and accepting the situation.
jokes.punchline: Frank is still genuinely confused by the basic biology of the surrogacy arrangement, trying to work out genetics aloud, with Dennis offering to explain later as if it's his problem to solve.
jokes.explanation: Good Frank confusion beat. His attempt to work out 'the mother is the father and the father is black and the baby's not black' aloud as a logic puzzle is consistent with his character. 'I'll talk you through it later' from Dennis is a good straight-man line.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: If this kid is mine, I'm gonna blow my brains out.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Oh, he got zooted, man. He took an eight-ball to the dome.

jokes.text: Charlie advocates for the sewer again — 'Let's party in the sewer!' — as the episode's final escalation
jokes.setup: The gang is heading back to the bar.
jokes.punchline: Charlie proposes the sewer as the party destination, returning to the opening sewer bit as a bookend.
jokes.explanation: Good structural bookend — the episode opens and closes with Charlie's enthusiasm for the sewer. The callback works because the sewer bit was strong enough to merit revisiting. Charlie's total commitment to the sewer as a lifestyle is a nice through-line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We're gonna be the father of the baby now. We're gonna be the fathers. It has been decided, so sayeth Thor. Thor said it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The who?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Thor.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Who Thor?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Is that your Greek God reference?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's a Nordic God.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Let's party in the sewer!' — others try to redirect him, then Frank tries to bring up his ring story again, to groans.
jokes.setup: Everyone is piling out of the hospital to continue the party.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate pivot to sewer-partying revives the cold-open running gag; Frank tries to tell his ring-in-the-sewer story again, which everyone is already sick of despite it having come up only hours ago.
jokes.explanation: Good bookend callback. The episode opening with the sewer conversation and closing with everyone returning to it (and Frank's ring story already being a tired repeated anecdote) gives the episode a nice circular structure. The fact that Frank's ring story is 'getting old' despite this being the same day is a good piece of comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Carmen? What are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.line: I'm here to get my baby.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The tranny's the dad. Yeah!

jokes.text: Frank's ring story gets shut down — 'Is this the ring story again? I am getting real tired of the ring story.'
jokes.setup: Frank begins explaining his justification for sewer-hanging: 'Suppose there's a storm and a guy loses his ring...'
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately recognizes this as 'the ring story' — implying Frank has told this exact story many times before as his go-to sewer justification. The gang is 'getting real tired' of it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing gag. The reveal that Frank has 'a ring story' — a prepared narrative justifying sewer exploration — that he has told so many times it has its own name, is very funny. It implies this sewer debate is an ongoing dynamic in the gang's life. 'You got to come up with something else, Frank' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No. I was their surrogate. We used her sperm and a donor egg and then they just kind of - right up there and -

dialogue.speaker: Carmen
dialogue.line: We had a difficult time finding a surrogate, but Dee was a miracle to us.

jokes.text: Dee's final line: 'Ha-ha! Good one, Dee! She's back, baby, she's back!' — said to herself after making a mediocre 'like sewage' quip.
jokes.setup: Frank asks what you find in the sewer; Dee says 'like sewage' as a dismissive quip.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately congratulates herself on the comeback with 'Ha-ha! Good one, Dee!' and 'She's back, baby!' — treating a mediocre joke as evidence of her triumphant return to form after childbirth.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dee moment to close the episode. The gap between the quality of her joke ('like sewage' — not a great comeback) and her self-congratulation ('she's back, baby!') is the whole joke. It captures Dee's delusional self-regard perfectly. 'She's back, baby, she's back!' as a self-directed celebration is completely specific to Dee and very funny as a final beat. High character integration — this is pure, distilled Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dee, you tricked us?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: How did I trick you?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We were getting all pumped up about being this baby's dad. We were all keyed up for nothing.

tmdb_overview: Dee's blessed event is fast approaching but the father's identity remains a mystery---to the gang, at least. So they throw a party and invite all of Dee's former flings.
